meta.description: 245th CAOS is an expeditionary unit organized to rapidly deploy, establish, operate, and sustain combat airfield operations in austere, forward-deployed, contingency, or Agile Combat Employment (ACE) environments. The squadron integrates deployable Air Traffic Control (ATC), Airfield Management (AM), and Radar, Airfield, and Weather Systems (RAWS) maintenance to provide safe, expeditionary command-and-control of aircraft and airfield infrastructure.
meta.jhaNotes: No current Job Hazard Analysis attached to 245th CAOS.
meta.emergencyNumbers: Dial 911, State location as Mcentire and give building number or area on base.
meta.medicalFacility:
Base Clinic: 169th Medical Group (MDG) - Building 984
Acute Care and Emergency Room Service are not provided here at McEntire but are located in the local surrounding area. If you are injured and feel you are in need of an ambulance, call 911. ALL injuries are to be reported to your supervisor, the McEntire Med Group and Base Safety immediately, however, do not delay treatment. Members on Military orders of any kind will have their initial visits (Line of Duty approved) sent to Tricare for payment. Any/all follow-up care that you receive must be pre-authorized by the Military Medical Support Office (MMSO).
meta.evacuationRoute: Muster in the grass field between Building 1070 and Security Force Building.
meta.activeShooterMethods: Current Department of the Air Force and Department of War guidance directs individuals caught in an active shooter incident to execute the tiered response protocol: RUN, HIDE, FIGHT. If an escape path is clear, immediately evacuate (Run). If evacuation is not possible, conceal yourself, barricade entry points, and silence all electronic devices (Hide). As an absolute last resort when your life is in imminent danger, attempt to incapacitate the shooter using physical force and improvised weapons (Fight). Once safe, notify emergency responders (911 or Base Defense Operations Center [BDOC]).

meta.trafficSafetyNotes:
Wearing portable headphones, earphones, or other listening devices while operating a motor-vehicle, running, jogging, walking, bicycling, or skating (e.g. roller skates, roller blades, skateboards, etc.) on AF installation roadways is prohibited, with the exception of running/jogging on the approved AF Physical Fitness assessment route (see PTL or Supervision for further details). This does not include the use of hearing aids, nor does it negate the requirement for wearing hearing protective equipment where conditions dictate their use. EXCEPTION: Motorcycle helmet intercom system between operator and passenger is permitted.

Vehicle operators on an AF installation and operators of government owned, leased, or rented vehicles, on or off an AF installation, shall not use cell phones while the vehicle is in operation, except when using a hands-free device or hands-free operating mode. When possible, vehicle operators should pull over and place the vehicle in park before using any cell phone. Land Mobile Radios (LMR) are primarily listening devices and are not restricted. Cell phones and other devices, used only in push-to-talk (walkie-talkie, direct connection) mode are considered LMR if required and issued for the performance of official duties.

selectedModules.title: Fall Arrest Systems
selectedModules.reference: DAFMAN 91-203 - Air Force Occupational Safety, Fire and Health Standards, Chapter 13; 29 CFR 1910.66 - Powered platforms for building maintenance; 29 CFR 1926.503 - Training requirements
selectedModules.trainingRequirement: Train employees exposed to fall hazards to recognize fall hazards and the procedures to minimize them, including use and inspection of fall arrest systems.
selectedModules.afTrainingRequirement: Cover anchorage selection, rescue planning, and equipment inspections before personnel use personal fall arrest systems in assigned tasks.
selectedModules.trainingBasis: OSHA 2254 / Walking-Working Surfaces and Fall Protection
selectedModules.notes:
General Industry: In general industry, fall protection is required at 4 feet. The 4-foot rule applies to 
walking and working surfaces and requires every open-sided floor or platform 4 feet or more above 
adjacent floor or ground level to be guarded. This requirement also applies to wall openings, window 
wall openings at a stairway landing, floor, platform, or balcony, from which there is a drop of more than 4 feet, and where the bottom of the opening is less than 3 feet above the platform or landing. Every 
chute wall opening from which there is a drop of more than 4 feet shall also be guarded.
Construction: In the construction industry, fall protection is required at 6 feet

selectedModules.title: Ladder Safety
selectedModules.reference: DAFMAN 91-203 - Air Force Occupational Safety, Fire and Health Standards, Chapter 7
selectedModules.trainingRequirement: Train workers to inspect ladders before use, maintain three points of contact, set ladders on stable surfaces, and avoid overreaching or using damaged ladders.
selectedModules.afTrainingRequirement: Provide hands-on ladder safety training at first assignment, including local storage, damaged-tag procedures, and fall prevention expectations.
selectedModules.notes: Personnel who use ladders at working heights of six feet or more will be adequately trained in the care and use of different types of ladders. Training will be conducted IAW DAFMAN 91-203, Chapter 7. The supervisor, or a designated trainer, will conduct this training when a worker is first assigned and periodically as needed. 245 ATCS Safety will provide training and presentation materials.

selectedModules.title: Personal Protective Equipment (PPE)
selectedModules.reference: DAFMAN 91-203 - Air Force Occupational Safety, Fire and Health Standards, Chapter 14; 29 CFR Part 1910 - Occupational Safety and Health Standards (General Industry Standards) Subpart I; 29 CFR 1910.132; 29 CFR 1910.133; 29 CFR 1910.135; 29 CFR 1910.136; 29 CFR 1910.138
selectedModules.trainingRequirement: Train each affected worker on when PPE is necessary, what PPE is necessary, how to properly don, doff, adjust, and wear PPE, the limitations of assigned PPE, and the proper care, maintenance, useful life, and disposal of PPE. Require workers to demonstrate understanding and proper use before performing work requiring PPE, and retrain when workplace conditions, job assignments, PPE types, or worker knowledge gaps make prior training obsolete.
selectedModules.afTrainingRequirement: Use the work-center JHA, BE occupational health assessment, manufacturer instructions, DAFMAN 91-203 Chapter 14, and local safety office guidance to identify PPE requirements. Supervisors must ensure PPE is provided, used, cleaned, inspected, maintained in sanitary and serviceable condition, and documented in JSTO training records. Cover eye and face protection, head protection, foot protection, hand protection, protective clothing, and respiratory or hearing protection when those programs apply.
selectedModules.notes:
Hazards should be engineered out, isolated, guarded against, or a safer alternative used as a 
substitute whenever possible before considering the use of PPE. PPE devices alone should not be relied 
on to provide protection against hazards, but should be used in conjunction with guards, engineering 
controls, and sound manufacturing practices.
Supervisors shall conduct and document hazard assessments in each workplace where their 
employees are performing duties. If PPE is required, the supervisor shall ensure that PPE is provided, 
used and maintained in a sanitary serviceable condition. They are responsible for maintaining discipline 
with regard to personnel wearing properly fitted PPE, when required, and shall consult the installation 
Ground Safety office and BE concerning the selection and use of PPE. 
Personal Protective Equipment (PPE). PPE shall be used whenever there are hazards that can do 
bodily harm through absorption, inhalation or physical contact. This equipment includes respiratory protective devices, special clothing and protective devices for the eyes, face, head, torso and 
extremities. All PPE shall be approved for the work performed and shall be maintained in satisfactory 
condition. The installation Ground Safety office and BE shall be consulted.

selectedModules.title: Hazardous Energy Control
selectedModules.reference: DAFMAN 91-203 - Air Force Occupational Safety, Fire and Health Standards, Chapter 21; 29 CFR 1910.147 - The control of hazardous energy (lockout/tagout)
selectedModules.trainingRequirement: Train authorized employees to recognize hazardous energy sources, the type and magnitude of energy present, and the methods and means for isolation and control. Train affected employees on the purpose and use of lockout/tagout procedures, and instruct all other employees on the prohibition against restarting locked or tagged equipment.
selectedModules.afTrainingRequirement: Document initial and refresher training when job assignments, machines, processes, or energy control procedures change, or when inspections show employee knowledge gaps.
selectedModules.notes:
Installation of Lockout/Tagout devices shall be performed by authorized personnel only.

Lockout is the preferred method of isolating machines or equipment from energy sources.  Tags are warning devices attached to energy isolating devices, and do not provide the physical restraint on those devices that is provided by a lock.  

When a lock or tag is attached to an energy isolating device, only the supervisor and the authorized personnel who initially installed the lock or tag can remove it. It can never be bypassed, ignored, or otherwise defeated.

A tag will be used in conjunction with the lock. AF Form 979, Danger Tag, will be used for immediate danger. AF Form 980, Caution Tag, will be used to warn personnel against potential hazards. AF Form 981, Out of Order Tag, will be used for indicating that a piece of equipment, machinery, or system is out of order. AF Form 982, Do Not Start Tag, will be used to alert personnel of hazards associated with starting equipment. This tag is used for a short time until an energy-isolating device can be installed.  

No attempt shall be made to override any energy isolation device when it is locked or tagged out. Doing so will result in severe discipline and potential termination of employment.  

For more information on Lockout/Tagout refer to DAFMAN 91-203, Chapter 21. For information on training refer to Part II.

selectedModules.title: Fire Protection and Prevention
selectedModules.reference: DAFMAN 91-203 - Air Force Occupational Safety, Fire and Health Standards; local fire prevention plan
selectedModules.trainingRequirement: Train personnel on fire hazards, reporting procedures, extinguisher locations, evacuation routes, pull stations, and local emergency response actions.
selectedModules.afTrainingRequirement: Use the JSTO and local fire prevention plan to brief workers on work-center fire hazards, alarm reporting, extinguisher use, and evacuation accountability.
selectedModules.notes:
Supervisors shall establish and maintain a training and certification system to ensure employees are trained and understand their fire prevention and protection responsibilities in their work areas. This training and certification system shall include documented annual training of employees, including fire extinguisher training and location of fire extinguishers, and immediate indoctrination of newly hired employees.

Initial and annual training will be conducted IAW DAFMAN 91-203 as well as NFPA 101, The Life Safety Code. Training is offered through Advanced Distance Learning System (ADLS) under the miscellaneous folder. For further information on Fire Extinguisher training, refer to Part II.

If an escape path is clear, immediately evacuate (Run). If evacuation is not possible, conceal yourself, barricade entry points, and silence all electronic devices (Hide). As an absolute last resort when your life is in imminent danger, attempt to incapacitate the shooter using physical force and improvised weapons (Fight). selectedModules.title: Fetal Protection Program
selectedModules.trainingRequirement: Provide job-specific hazard awareness for reproductive health risks where occupational exposures may affect pregnant workers or fetuses.
selectedModules.afTrainingRequirement: Use occupational and environmental health guidance to discuss declaration options, exposure review, and local work restriction procedures.
selectedModules.notes:
Workers in industrial workplaces may have potential exposures to hazards that can affect their reproductive health. There are hazards present to both male and female employees that affect the ability to reproduce as well as the normal and healthy development of a fetus.  Reproductive Health Training is a one-time training requirement that is required as part of an employee’s Initial Job Safety Training. Outlines for this training are provided by Public Health. If new workplace hazards are introduced that pose a significant threat to the employee’s reproductive health, additional workplace specific training will be required.

Training will be conducted IAW AFI 44-102, Medical Care Management, AFI 48-145, Occupational and Environmental Health Program, and ANGI 40-104, Pregnancy of Air National Guard Personnel. In addition to the one-time training requirement, female workers that become pregnant must report their pregnancy to the Public Health office at the MDG as soon as reasonably possible, but NLT than the first UTA for traditional members or within 5 workdays for full-time employees. Supervisors must ensure this training is accomplished and that pregnant members report immediately to the MDG. The MDG will perform a pregnancy profile evaluation to determine potential hazards of the workplace as well as restrictions to protect the employee and their fetus. Supervisors must ensure that members are following their duty restrictions. Pregnant members must report any changes in medical status to the MDG immediately.

selectedModules.title: Jewelry / Loose Articles Restrictions
selectedModules.trainingRequirement: Train workers on removing jewelry and securing loose articles when working around machinery, electrical hazards, rotating equipment, or snag hazards.
selectedModules.afTrainingRequirement: Use local work-center restrictions and equipment guidance to define prohibited items and exceptions for mission-essential tasks.
selectedModules.notes:
Mishap statistics over the past 10 years have revealed that the loss of portions of fingers due to the ring catching on some object is one of the most frequent causes of lost-time permanent partial inju¬ries. Because of the potential for serious injury, finger rings will not be worn by personnel engaged in the following activities. This restriction is also extended to personnel who may be assigned to these tasks on an infrequent basis.
NOTE: This prohibition applies only to personnel actually performing the work and is not intended for administrative and support personnel assigned to or visiting these areas. But remember, if the employee is involved in any of the activities then the prohibition DOES apply.

•	Climbing, ascending, or descending activi¬ties where personnel could fall or jump from elevated surfaces account for the majority of injuries caused by the finger ring catching on an object.  Some examples include personnel working on elevated surfaces: i.e., ladders, scaffolds, platforms, roofs, high reach vehicles, or descending from large ve¬hicles such as refuelers, wreckers, sweepers, dump trucks, and stake bed trucks. The stake bed truck has been associated with a large majority of injuries caused by personnel jumping or descending from a large vehicle.
•	Most materials handling operations.
•	Work activities where personnel are ex¬posed to moving machinery, rotating or revolving part, or any task that could result in hands being caught in moving parts.  Remove rings/jewelry when using the paper shredder!
•	Work activities where personnel are exposed to energized electrical circuits.

WARNING: Placing tape over rings or wearing gloves on the hand with a ring does not provide protection or eliminate the requirement to remove finger rings.

Other Jewelry: Any jewelry that presents a potential for catching, snagging, pulling, and tearing should be evaluated and restricted from wear if necessary. Some types of jewelry that should be controlled under these job situations are watches, bracelets, and necklaces. Whenever pos¬sible, these types of jewelry should be removed before entering work areas where jewelry hazards exist.

Jewelry will not be worn while working on or around any equipment. It’s a wise practice to remove all rings at the beginning of your shift and store them in your personal locker.

selectedModules.title: Hearing Conservation
selectedModules.trainingRequirement: Train noise-exposed employees annually on the effects of noise, the purpose of hearing protectors, the advantages and disadvantages of various protectors, and the purpose of audiometric testing.
selectedModules.afTrainingRequirement: Ensure workers enrolled in hearing conservation understand noise hazard areas, double-hearing protection requirements, and local follow-up actions tied to occupational health evaluations.
selectedModules.notes:
Identified workers with a determined occupational exposure to hazardous noise will be enrolled in the HCP, complete annual HCP Training, and receive annual audiograms. This audiogram is tracked and maintained by PH no further documentation is required of shop level personnel. Personnel not enrolled in the HCP, but exposed to possible noise hazards will receive a one-time Hearing Protection Awareness Training from their supervisor. 
Supervisors must protect the hearing of assigned personnel by ensuring protective engineering and administrative controls are implemented. PPE must be provided and used by all workers. Supervisors must ensure the workplace complies with all OSHA, DoD, and AF HCP requirements.

selectedModules.title: Flight Line Driving
selectedModules.reference: DAFMAN 91-203 - Air Force Occupational Safety, Fire and Health Standards, Chapter 24
selectedModules.trainingRequirement: Provide local flight line driving rules, markings, vehicle lighting requirements, restricted areas, and aircraft hazard awareness before granting driving privileges.
selectedModules.afTrainingRequirement: Use installation or unit-approved training and certification for airfield/fight line operations, to include local speed, spotter, and no-lone-zone requirements.
selectedModules.afTrainingBasis: DAFMAN 91-203 / Aircraft Flight Line – Ground Operations and Activities
selectedModules.notes:
The safe operation of all government and civilian motor vehicles on the flight line is absolutely essential to normal aircraft operations and maintenance. Motor vehicles present a clear and definite danger to aircraft and ground personnel. Carelessness, haste, and disregard for established safety standards are the primary causes of high accident potential (HAP) incidents, aircraft-vehicle mishaps, and personnel injury on the flight line.
The 245th CAOS has a very limited number of personnel that need/possess this training, but none are required. Flight line driving is done annually on ADLS and trained with 169 OG/AM Airfield Management.

selectedModules.title: Government Vehicle / Utility Vehicle Use
selectedModules.trainingRequirement: Train vehicle operators on seat belts, speed limits, local traffic hazards, spotter use while backing, and restrictions on electronic device use while driving.
selectedModules.afTrainingRequirement: Brief operators on unit-specific government vehicle training requirements, local route restrictions, low-speed vehicle rules, and documentation of qualification.
selectedModules.trainingBasis: OSHA 2254 / Vehicle and Mobile Equipment Concepts
selectedModules.notes:
Training outlines for each piece of equipment (LSV, 4x4 Truck, HMMWV, etc) will be accomplished by the shop according to instructions in AFI 24-301, Vehicle Operations. The training outline (course content) will include formal instruction; hands-on demonstrations by the instructor with practical exercises performed by the trainee; and an evaluation of the trainee ‘s performance which confirms the operator‘s knowledge of equipment operations and service instructions.

In addition to initial training and certification, a qualified instructor shall evaluate each operator at least once every three years and provide refresher training in relevant topics anytime there is reason to believe there is a need.

selectedModules.title: Manual Lifting and Material Handling
selectedModules.reference: DAFMAN 91-203 - Air Force Occupational Safety, Fire and Health Standards, Chapter 20
selectedModules.trainingRequirement: Train workers on proper lifting techniques, team lifting, load assessment, and use of lifting aids to reduce musculoskeletal injury risk.
selectedModules.afTrainingRequirement: Provide verbal and written guidance on manual lifting, lifting devices, and local reporting actions for strain or overexertion symptoms.
selectedModules.trainingBasis: OSHA 2254 / Ergonomics and Material Handling Concepts
selectedModules.notes:
Back injuries are a leading cause of lost work time. Not using proper lifting techniques can lead to a painful and debilitating back injury. Always consider the load you’re about to lift and never over-exert yourself! DAFMAN 91-203, AF Occupational Safety, Fire & Health Standards, covers lifting techniques in details. There are three basic methods of lifting, that is, straight back-bent knees, free style, and kinetic. Each has advan¬tages and limitations. The kinetic method is the most widely accepted and taught because it provides more stability for the worker while reducing load on the back muscles and intervertebral disks.
 •	Position feet correctly. Place feet far enough apart for balance with one foot to the rear of the object and the other foot slightly ahead of the other and to the side of the object.
•	Crouch close to the load. Crouching is preferred to squatting. Stay close to the load to minimize strain on the back muscles.
•	Pick up materials with a full palm grip. Do not attempt to pick up weights with a fingertip grip. Ensure that the load is free of grease or sharp points which could cause injury. Use suitable gloves when necessary.
•	Always keep the back as straight as possible. It may not be possible to keep the back in the vertical plane but avoid arching the back. Bend from the hips and not from the middle of the back.
•	With the arms, slide the ob¬ject toward the body to give it some motion (kinetic energy). At the same time, use the legs to lift the object and bring the back to a vertical position. Keep the object close to the body while lifting.

Acceptable carrying methods differ, based upon the type of material, distance, and number of workers. Workers should be instructed during initial train¬ing in each procedure (for example, neck, shoulder, side, tray, two-person, and under-arm carry methods, etc.).
